summary: Describes a protocol for configuring SSH public keys in an implementation-independent way. SSH authenticates users by public key but defined no mechanism to distribute them, and no common solution exists.

eli5.summary: SSH can check you by a key, but nobody said how to hand the keys to servers. This defines a standard way to add and remove those keys.

subtitle: A small SSH subsystem that lets a logged-in user add, remove and list their own public keys on a server.

tldr.problem: SSH can authenticate users by public key but defines no way to get keys onto the server, so every implementation does it differently.
tldr.mechanism: A subsystem named publickey runs over an authenticated SSH session and offers four operations (add, remove, list, listattributes), with optional attributes that restrict how a key may be used.
tldr.outcome: Client software can manage a user's keys the same way on any server that implements it. The RFC has since been updated by RFC 9519.

today: RFC 4819 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 9519.

sections.title: Why a Public Key Subsystem
sections.content:
Secure Shell defines public-key user authentication but no mechanism for key distribution. Common practice is to log in once with a password and transfer the public key to the server, yet no two implementations use the same way to configure a key.

This RFC describes a subsystem that configures public keys in an implementation-independent way, so client software can take on the burden. It is designed for extreme simplicity and is explicitly not a replacement for PKIX. It runs on top of the SSH transport and user authentication protocols and is used from the SSH Connection Protocol as a subsystem named publickey. The user must already be able to authenticate; if password authentication is used, servers SHOULD offer an option to disable it after the first public key is added.
sections.eli5: Everyone used to hand over keys in their own odd way. This gives one common way, like all shops agreeing on how to hand out spare keys.

sections.title: Opening the Subsystem
sections.content:
The subsystem lets clients add, remove and list public keys. The keys it handles are specific to, and limited to, the authenticated user. Requests go to the server as packets, and the server sends response packets that indicate success or failure plus any data.

To start it, the client sends an SSH_MSG_CHANNEL_REQUEST with request type subsystem and the name publickey on an existing session channel. If the client asked for a reply, the server MUST answer SSH_MSG_CHANNEL_SUCCESS or SSH_MSG_CHANNEL_FAILURE. The server SHOULD fail it if the user is not allowed access, for example because they authenticated with a restricted public key. Clients are RECOMMENDED to request and check the reply.
sections.eli5: You knock on a special door marked "publickey" inside the building you already got into. If you are not allowed in that room, the door stays shut.

sections.title: Packets, Status and Version
sections.content:
Every request and response has the form uint32 length, string name, then data specific to that name. The client MUST receive acknowledgement of each request before sending the next. A request is acknowledged by a status packet holding a status code, a description and a language tag; if there is response data, the status comes after it. A status MUST be sent for unrecognized packets.

Both sides MUST begin by sending a version packet. This RFC describes version 2 (version 1 was used by an early draft). Each side sends the highest version it implements and the lower number is used. If a side cannot support it, it SHOULD send status SSH_PUBLICKEY_VERSION_NOT_SUPPORTED and close the subsystem. This is the only time a client sends a status message. The version packet MUST NOT be sent again.
sections.eli5: First both sides say which rulebook edition they know and agree to use the older one. After that, every question gets an answer saying "done" or what went wrong.

sections.title: Add, Remove, List and Listattributes
sections.content:
The subsystem defines four operations. add sends the key algorithm name, the key blob, an overwrite flag and a list of attributes (name, value, critical flag). The server MUST store the key so it can be used for later authentication. If overwrite is false and the key exists, it MUST return SSH_PUBLICKEY_KEY_ALREADY_PRESENT; if overwrite is true but the key cannot be overwritten, SSH_PUBLICKEY_ACCESS_DENIED. If the server does not implement a critical attribute it MUST fail the add with SSH_PUBLICKEY_ATTRIBUTE_NOT_SUPPORTED; merely storing it is not enough.

remove sends the algorithm name and key blob, and the server MUST remove that key so it cannot authenticate later. list returns zero or more publickey responses in no particular order, followed by a status packet; implementations SHOULD support it. listattributes returns zero or more attribute responses, each with a compulsory flag showing whether the server applies that attribute to all added keys because of administrative settings, then a status packet. Supporting it is optional.
sections.eli5: You can hand in a new key, take one back, ask to see all your keys, or ask what special rules the door understands.

sections.title: Key Attributes
sections.content:
Attributes attach restrictions or notes to a key. comment holds user text in UTF-8 that the server must not act upon, and comment-language must immediately follow a comment. Neither should be critical.

Restrictions, mostly marked SHOULD be critical, include command-override (run a fixed command instead of any requested shell or command; empty denies both), subsystem (a comma-separated list of allowed subsystems), x11, shell, exec, agent and env (deny that kind of request), from (a comma-separated list of hosts the key may be used from; others MUST be denied), port-forward (only listed hosts for direct-tcpip) and reverse-forward (only listed ports for tcpip-forward).

Servers MAY also let administrators enforce certain attributes compulsorily. Names can be extended locally with the form name@domainname.
sections.eli5: A key can come with rules attached, such as "only works from this computer" or "can only run this one task". The server must either follow a rule or refuse the key.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The protocol assumes it runs over a secure channel with authenticated endpoints, and so is externally protected from network-level attacks. Because it lets authentication data be uploaded and changed, the server must enforce access controls. Users can overwrite an existing key with fewer restrictions than before, so servers should take care that clients cannot override presets set by the administrator.

Clients must also trust the server to implement attributes correctly; a server bug could authorize a key for more access than intended or apply fewer restrictions.
sections.eli5: Because this lets you change who may enter, the server must double-check what you are allowed to change, and you have to trust it to follow your rules.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
The RFC registers the subsystem name publickey and creates registries for request names, response names, attribute names and status codes. Names must be printable US-ASCII, must not contain at-sign, comma, whitespace or control characters, are case-sensitive and at most 64 characters. New names need IETF Consensus.

Status codes range from 0 to 255. New codes in the range 0 to 191 need Standards Action, and 192 to 255 is private use. The initial codes run from SSH_PUBLICKEY_SUCCESS (0) to SSH_PUBLICKEY_ATTRIBUTE_NOT_SUPPORTED (9).
sections.eli5: There is an official list of the words this protocol uses so nobody invents clashing ones, plus a private corner for personal extras.
